subject: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code

messages.author: 4b681bcd9d4d425d
messages.subject: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code
parts:
Hi all,

I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.

As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.

Specific Questions:
1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?

2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)

3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?

4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features? 

Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
David Manheim

The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code
parts:
Hi David,

I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to 
be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.  

So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates). 

I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.

I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.

Krzysztof

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code
parts:
I should note that I got the SIR models fitting robustly by
setting the initial step size to a small value.  The problem
with these models is that the tails in which you tend to
explore in warmup lead to stiff systems which freeze the 
Boost ODE solver.  Setting the sampler step size to a small 
value initially prevents the extreme steps that can lead the
sampler into these regimes and worked pretty robustly in
my experience.

That said, we not have CVODES for truly stiff systems and
the Boost ODE solver will bail after a set number of iterations
so you shouldn’t see freezing anymore.

Priors are indeed important for these models as the nonlinearities
in the ODEs tend to induce some nasty non-identifiabilities,
especially when you’re measuring only a few components.

messages.author: 4b681bcd9d4d425d
messages.subject: Re: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code
parts:
Hi Krzysztof,

These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.

Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)

The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)

Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!

Thanks for the suggestions,
David

Krzysztof

David

parts:
Hi,

Yes, I was involved in the Dengue modeling project, though good prediction was pretty intractable given the lack of information available; for high fidelity modeling you need lots of location, population, and geography specific data. Some cool ML approaches were tried by various teams with some success, but they require years and years of data to train, and aren't applicable to new locations or changing conditions, so there is limited policy relevance. (And the sponsors basically said they weren't hopeful that Dengue modeling could be advanced all that much.)

I have asked before about time varying inputs, and it's (appropriately) not high on the list of priorities for the core team. I'll be trying gamma priors - my first trial seems to have gotten fairly good convergence, without much fiddling, but that may be luck.

Cheers,
David

Hi David,

I have started looking at your code in a bit more detail. I notice for example that you have

Overall_Infection_Total[y] <- rep_array(0.001,N_t);

and a comment above

//Init to non-0, try to banish some nan error messages in lognormal later. (Low count, Ignore it for now.)

You may now have banished the nan error messages :-) You also say you are now using gamma priors and getting convergence. Do you have a git (or other) repo of the latest version of your code? I'd quite like to investigate this but I'd rather not solve any problems you have already put to bed.

Many thanks, Dominic.

On Thursday, 14 July 2016 04:18:01 UTC+2, David Manheim wrote:
Hi,

Yes, I was involved in the Dengue modeling project, though good prediction was pretty intractable given the lack of information available; for high fidelity modeling you need lots of location, population, and geography specific data. Some cool ML approaches were tried by various teams with some success, but they require years and years of data to train, and aren't applicable to new locations or changing conditions, so there is limited policy relevance. (And the sponsors basically said they weren't hopeful that Dengue modeling could be advanced all that much.)

I have asked before about time varying inputs, and it's (appropriately) not high on the list of priorities for the core team. I'll be trying gamma priors - my first trial seems to have gotten fairly good convergence, without much fiddling, but that may be luck.

Cheers,
David

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 9:57:13 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
Thanks for sharing!  A few comments below. K

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 4:28:31 PM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
Hi Krzysztof,

These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.

Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)

Thanks for mentioning the report, were you involved in the dengue modeling exercise?
 

The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)

Thanks for sharing your experience with this.  The systematic patterns in residuals is another feature likely to cause computational problems so it may be a place where introducing time-varying parameters would improve algorithm efficiency enough to offset the extra computational cost.  It would be great to have a plug-in component like the birthday data model for this! Seems like everyone has to re-invent the wheel for dealing with big shocks from holidays.  
 

Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!

I tend to use gamma priors (and generally spend a lot of time simulating to get the right parameters) or just do more or less standard normal priors and use a scaled logit to get them to cover the right range nicely.  Then you just need to check posterior results to make sure you're not bumping up against the upper end of the range.  There are divergent opinions on this around here so hopefully others will chime in with alternatives but in terms of taking care of computational problems the scaled logit trick works really well as long as you don't have strong background knowledge indicating that values extremely close to zero are likely.
 
Krzysztof


Thanks for the suggestions,
David

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 2:07:53 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
Hi David,

I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to 
be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.  

So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates). 

I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.

I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.

Krzysztof

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 11:53:36 AM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
Hi all,

I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.

As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.

Specific Questions:
1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?

2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)

3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?

4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features? 

Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
David Manheim

The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.
